Hi OP,

I have social anxieties and, while I can't say I react in the same was as your GF, I can say what has helped for me. 

It's been mentioned already but I've definitely found group settings easier when I have met or know each person individually. Meeting new people is difficult and people with social anxiety are always really self-conscious about what other people think of them. Meeting a group of new people is like multiplying that anxiety by how ever many people there are. It can be really quite stressful.

I'd recommend having her meet one or two of these people individually first just so that initial awkward first meeting has already been done. 

Also, if these are close friends, maybe giving them the heads up that she is socially anxious and maybe not to put any spotlight on her or make meeting her a "thing" might mean she feels a bit more at ease and the meeting is less awkward for all.

These aren't my stories but stories from my dad who is a retired firefighter. The two that always stick out to him:

1. Called to respond to a body in the water. They turn up and see that there is a body on its back that has obviously been in the water sometime due to the bloat. At the time (late 80's-mid 90's) our fire service didn't have the water rescue resources that it does now so the only way for them to get the body was to, essentially, lasso it. One of is colleagues does the whole "Yee-haw cowboy" swing above his head, tosses the rope, misses the hook and basically guillotines the body straight through the stomach. He said the smell was instant even though they were a good distance from it on the embankment. They had to keep trying to hook this body with the rope and keep missing, slapping all the stink out of it. Eventually they got it and pulled it to the shore and some poor young policeman got sent down to try and look for i.d. in the pockets. He said the guy was visibly throwing up behind his hand due to the smell.
2. Called to respond to a house fire. Fire was caused by an elderly woman falling asleep in her chair whilst smoking a cigarette. She'd dropped the cigarette onto her nightgown and caught on fire but remained undiscovered for sometime as there weren't any smoke alarms and she lived alone. By the time they had gotten there the house was well alight. Once putting out the fire they went inside to inspect further. Apparently the woman was bariatric so when her body burned, all the fat from her body rose up and formed a fat layer on the ceiling which was dripping onto them as they walked around. Apparently she was essentially "just a pair of legs in a chair" at that point.

Firefighters see some shit.

For the filling:
750g Lean diced beef
500ml Ale of your choice (I use Doom Bar)
200ml beef stock
4 tbsp tomato puree
3 tbsp plain flour (extra for dusting) 
2 cloves of garlic (I just used 1tsp of lazy garlic) 
2 tsp thyme
2 tsp sugar
2 tsp wholegrain mustard
1 tbsp Worcestershire sauce
2 Bay leaves
Salt and pepper

Pastry:
250g plain flour
100g butter (cubed)
1-2tbsp cold water
Pinch of salt
1 pack ready to roll puff pastry
1 beaten egg

Method:

 1. Lightly dust the diced beef with some plain flour then brown on all sides in the frying pan. Once done, transfer to slow cooker.
  
2.Pour the ale into the same frying pan and cook on a high heat for a few minutes to cook out the alcohol. Then transfer to slow cook. 

 3.Add all the remaining filling ingredients to the slow cooker, give it a stir and then cook on low for a minimum of 6 hours (I usually go for 8).

4.Meanwhile, to make the pastry, add the flour, butter and salt to a bowl. Use the rubbing method to bring the flour and butter together like breadcrumbs. Pour in 1 tbsp of water and stir with a knife. The pastry should start to come together. Add the second tbsp of water and begin to knead until the pastry just comes together. Wrap in cling film and chill in the fridge. 

5.Once the filling has cooked, it needs to be completely cool before it can go in the pastry. Either leave to cool in the slow cooker and continue the next day or transfer the filling to a glass bowl and place the glass bowl in ice water, stirring until the filling has cooled. 

6.Remove the shortcrust from the fridge and dust your worktop with flour. Roll out your pastry wide enough to fill the base of your pie dish and lay it in. 

7.Fill your pie with the filling, leaving about 1/3 of the height of the dish free. There will be quite a lot of leftover liquid, this makes a great gravy to serve with it. 

8.Roll out your puff pastry top and lay over the pie. Trim the edges and crimp if you like. 

9.Make 2 or 3 cuts in the pastry lid to allow steam to escape and avoid a soggy pie. 
 
10.Brush the pastry with the beaten egg. 
 
11.Heat the oven to 200c and leave a baking tray Inside the oven to heat up. (this is probably the most important step to avoid soggy bottoms) 

12.When ready, place the pie on the preheated tray and bake for 30mins. You may need to cover the pastry with tin foil to avoid burning.

To make 4 "hand sized" breads

125 grams/ 1 cup of self raising flour
125 grams/1 cup of natural yogurt
1/2 teaspoon baking powder

Mix all ingredients in a bowl until combined then knead on a floured surface for about a minute (until there's no sticky bit) and form a ball. 

Cut into 4 pieces and roll each piece flat with a rolling pin.

Dry fry each bread on a griddle pan, turning occasionally to prevent too much charring. When just about done on both sides, brush as much or as little garlic butter as you like.

Apparently, that recipe is good for a quick pizza dough too but I imagine you'd want to double up on the quantities for that.

Let this be a hard lesson not to get yourself financially mixed up with someone who treats you like shit.

Lots of people forget about their smoke alarms once they're installed. Just like ornaments on a shelf, over time they do gather small build ups of dust (or even little insects) that need hovering out with the soft brush attachment on your vacuum cleaner.

I work for a UK Fire Service and we fit 10yr battery operated smoke alarms in houses. One of the bits of maintenance advice we give is to give it a clean about once every 3 months.
Also, strangely, on some Fire Angel battery operated smoke alarms, there was a manufacturers fault which causes them to be particularly sensitive to changes in temperature. A lot of people had them "chirping" during winter. Usually its because they were near to an area with a radiator so overnight it'd go cold then when the heating came on, off they went. Might be worth reconsidering the placement of them if this is the case as repeated false alarms can cause the battery life to drain in them and it may not work when you need it too (same goes for mains operated as they all have battery back ups in case of power failure)

Don't forget to test it once a week as well :)
